title: Explorers or boys messing about?
author: Steven Morris
blurb: A news article about a costly helicopter rescue in Antarctica. Morris uses irony and scepticism to ask whether these men are really explorers.
source: by Steven Morris - Adapted from The Guardian, 28 January 2003
heading: Explorers or boys messing about? Either way, taxpayer gets rescue bill
standfirst: Helicopter duo plucked from liferaft after Antarctic crash

paragraphs.html: Their last expedition ended in farce when the Russians threatened to send in military planes to intercept them as they tried to cross into Siberia via the icebound Bering Strait.
Yesterday a new adventure undertaken by British explorers Steve Brooks and Quentin Smith almost led to tragedy when their helicopter plunged into the sea off Antarctica.

The men were plucked from the icy water by a Chilean naval ship after a nine-hour rescue which began when Mr Brooks contacted his wife, Jo Vestey, on his satellite phone asking for assistance. The rescue involved the Royal Navy, the RAF and British coastguards.
Last night there was resentment in some quarters that the men's adventure had cost the taxpayers of Britain and Chile tens of thousands of pounds.
Experts questioned the wisdom of taking a small helicopter — the four-seater Robinson R44 has a single engine — into such a hostile environment.

There was also confusion about what exactly the men were trying to achieve. A website set up to promote the Bering Strait expedition claims the team were planning to fly from the north to south pole in their "trusty helicopter".
But Ms Vestey claimed she did not know what the pair were up to, describing them as "boys messing about with a helicopter".

The drama began at around 1am British time when Mr Brooks, 42, and 40-year-old Mr Smith, also known as Q, ditched into the sea 100 miles off Antarctica, about 36 miles north of Smith Island, and scrambled into their liferaft.
Mr Brooks called his wife in London on his satellite phone. She said: "He said they were both in the liferaft but were okay and could I call the emergency people?"
Meanwhile, distress signals were being beamed from the ditched helicopter and from Mr Brooks' Breitling emergency watch, a wedding present.
The signals from the aircraft were deciphered by Falmouth coastguard and passed on to the rescue coordination centre at RAF Kinloss in Scotland.
The Royal Navy's ice patrol ship, HMS Endurance, which was 180 miles away surveying uncharted waters, began steaming towards the scene and dispatched its two Lynx helicopters.
One was driven back because of poor visibility but the second was on its way when the men were picked up by a Chilean naval vessel at about 10.20am British time.
Though the pair wore survival suits and the weather at the spot where they ditched was clear, one Antarctic explorer told Mr Brooks' wife it was "nothing short of a miracle" that they had survived.

Both men are experienced adventurers. Mr Brooks, a property developer from London, has taken part in expeditions to 70 countries in 15 years. He has trekked solo to Everest base camp and walked barefoot for three days in the Himalayas. He has negotiated the white water rapids of the Zambezi river by kayak and survived a charge by a silver back gorilla in the Congo. He is also a qualified mechanical engineer and pilot.
He and his wife spent their honeymoon flying the helicopter from Alaska to Chile. The 16,000-mile trip took three months.
Mr Smith, also from London, claims to have been flying since the age of five. He has twice flown a helicopter around the globe and won the world freestyle helicopter flying championship.
Despite their experience, it is not the first time they have hit the headlines for the wrong reasons.

In April, Mr Brooks and another explorer, Graham Stratford, were poised to become the first to complete a crossing of the 56-mile wide frozen Bering Strait between the US and Russia in an amphibious vehicle, Snowbird VI, which could carve its way through ice floes and float in the water in between.
But they were forced to call a halt after the Russian authorities told them they would scramble military helicopters to lift them off the ice if they crossed the border.
Ironically, one of the aims of the expedition, for which Mr Smith provided air back-up, was to demonstrate how good relations between east and west had become.

The wisdom of the team's latest adventure was questioned by, among others, Günter Endres, editor of Jane's Helicopter Markets and Systems, said: "I'm surprised they used the R44. I wouldn't use a helicopter like that to go so far over the sea. It sounds as if they were pushing it to the maximum".
A spokesman for the pair said it was not known what had gone wrong. The flying conditions had been "excellent".
The Ministry of Defence said the taxpayer would pick up the bill, as was normal in rescues in the UK and abroad. The spokesperson said it was "highly unlikely" it would recover any of the money.

Last night the men were on their way to the Chilean naval base Eduardo Frei, where HMS Endurance was to pick them up. Ms Vestey said: "They have been checked and appear to be well. I don't know what will happen to them once they have been picked up by HMS Endurance — they'll probably have their bottoms kicked and be sent home the long way".

opening-hook.what: Starting with 'ended in farce' immediately undermines the explorers' credibility. The word 'farce' sets a mocking tone before we even learn about the current incident.
opening-hook.effect: Sets skeptical tone from the start, priming readers to view the explorers as incompetent.

dramatic-threat.quote: threatened to send in military planes
dramatic-threat.what: 'Threatened to send in military planes' creates an image of international incident and incompetence.
dramatic-threat.effect: Makes their previous expedition sound like it caused serious diplomatic problems.

icebound.what: 'Icebound' emphasises the harsh, frozen conditions they repeatedly choose to enter unprepared.
icebound.effect: Highlights the dangerous environment they keep entering recklessly.

time-marker.what: 'Yesterday' creates immediacy and news urgency, linking this failure to their pattern of mishaps.
time-marker.effect: Makes the story immediate and newsworthy while connecting to past failures.

new-adventure.what: Calling it a 'new adventure' when it ends in disaster creates irony - their adventures are disasters.
new-adventure.effect: The word 'adventure' becomes ironic given the outcome.

almost-tragedy.what: 'Almost led to tragedy' emphasises how close to death they came, implying recklessness.
almost-tragedy.effect: Highlights the life-threatening consequences of their poor judgment.

dramatic-verb.what: 'Plunged' is more dramatic than 'crashed' or 'landed', emphasising violence and lack of control.
dramatic-verb.effect: Makes the crash sound violent and uncontrolled.

rescue-verb.what: 'Plucked' makes them seem helpless, like objects being retrieved rather than competent explorers.
rescue-verb.effect: Reduces them to passive objects needing rescue.

icy-water.what: 'Icy water' emphasises the lethal environment they put themselves in.
icy-water.effect: Reminds readers of the deadly conditions.

duration-emphasis.what: 'Nine-hour' highlights the extensive time required, building the case about waste before mentioning money.
duration-emphasis.effect: Shows the extensive resources and time needed for their rescue.

tripling.quote: the Royal Navy, the RAF and British coastguards
tripling.what: Listing three services (Royal Navy, RAF, British coastguards) emphasises the scale of resources needed.
tripling.effect: Emphasises how many organisations had to help.

resentment.what: 'Resentment' is stronger than 'concern' or 'questions' - it shows active anger from the public.
resentment.effect: Shows public anger, not just concern.

cost-emphasis.quote: the taxpayers of Britain and Chile tens of thousands of pounds
cost-emphasis.what: 'Tens of thousands of pounds' puts a specific price on their adventure for taxpaying readers.
cost-emphasis.effect: Makes the cost concrete and personal to taxpayers.

experts.what: Starting with 'Experts' brings professional judgment to criticise amateur adventurers.

wisdom.what: Questioning their 'wisdom' directly challenges their intelligence and decision-making.

small-helicopter.what: 'Small' emphasises the inadequacy of their equipment for such a journey.

single-engine.what: 'Single engine' highlights the specific danger - no backup if it fails over the ocean.
single-engine.effect: Shows specific technical risk they ignored.

hostile.what: 'Hostile environment' makes Antarctica seem actively aggressive, emphasising their poor judgment.

confusion.what: 'Confusion' suggests they lack clear goals - they're not serious explorers with a mission.
confusion.effect: Questions whether they even had a real plan.

trusty-irony.what: Quotation marks around 'trusty helicopter' signal Morris's skepticism - it just crashed.

did-not-know.what: Even his wife 'did not know' their plans, suggesting poor planning and communication.
did-not-know.effect: Shows lack of planning if wife doesn't know.

boys-messing.quote: boys messing about with a helicopter
boys-messing.what: 'Boys messing about' reduces them from men and explorers to children playing with toys.
boys-messing.effect: Infantilises grown men into irresponsible boys.

drama-begins.what: 'The drama began' shifts to storytelling mode, making it sound like unnecessary theatre.
drama-begins.effect: Makes it sound like theatrical performance, not serious exploration.

nickname.what: 'Also known as Q' adds James Bond pretension that seems absurd given their incompetence.
nickname.effect: James Bond reference seems pretentious given the failure.

ditched.what: 'Ditched' is technical aviation language for emergency water landing, adding authenticity.

distances.quote: 100 miles off Antarctica, about 36 miles north of Smith Island
distances.what: Specific distances ('100 miles... 36 miles') emphasise how far from help they were.
distances.effect: Shows how remote and dangerous their location was.

scrambled.what: 'Scrambled' suggests desperate, undignified panic rather than calm emergency response.
scrambled.effect: Suggests panic rather than calm professional response.

direct-quote.quote: He said they were both in the liferaft but were okay and could I call the emergency people?
direct-quote.what: The wife's matter-of-fact quote ('could I call the emergency people?') makes the life-threatening situation sound like calling a plumber.

luxury-detail.quote: Mr Brooks' Breitling emergency watch, a wedding present
luxury-detail.what: 'Breitling emergency watch, a wedding present' subtly highlights their wealth - they have expensive toys for their dangerous games.
luxury-detail.effect: Subtly highlights their privilege and wealth.

nautical-verb.what: 'Steaming' is proper nautical language, contrasting professional Navy response with amateur explorers.
nautical-verb.effect: Professional naval term contrasts with amateur explorers.

miracle-quote.what: An Antarctic explorer calling survival 'a miracle' emphasises how lucky they were, not how skilled.
miracle-quote.effect: Expert opinion emphasises luck over skill.

credentials.what: Morris waits until paragraph 15 to list their experience, after establishing them as incompetent - the structure undermines their achievements.
credentials.effect: Credentials come too late to change impression of incompetence.

class-marker.what: 'Property developer from London' signals wealth and privilege to Guardian readers, suggesting entitled rich men playing with danger.
class-marker.effect: Class marker suggesting privilege and entitlement.

impressive-detail.what: '16,000-mile trip took three months' sounds impressive but in context suggests they have too much time and money.
impressive-detail.effect: Impressive but suggests too much leisure time.

undermining-transition.what: 'Despite their experience' sets up the contradiction - all their experience doesn't prevent repeated failures.
undermining-transition.effect: Transition undermines all the credentials just listed.

pattern-criticism.quote: it is not the first time they have hit the headlines for the wrong reasons
pattern-criticism.what: 'Not the first time they have hit the headlines for the wrong reasons' establishes a pattern of failure and publicity-seeking.
pattern-criticism.effect: Establishes pattern of failure and attention-seeking.

failure-pattern.quote: they were forced to call a halt
failure-pattern.what: 'Forced to call a halt' shows another abandoned mission, reinforcing the pattern of incompetence.

ironically.what: 'Ironically' highlights the gap between their stated aims (showing good relations) and actual results (international incident).
ironically.effect: Points out the ironic failure of their mission.

expert-criticism.quote: The wisdom of the team's latest adventure was questioned by, among others, Günter Endres, editor of Jane's Helicopter Markets and Systems
expert-criticism.what: Citing the editor of Jane's Helicopter Markets adds authoritative weight to criticism of their judgment.

expert-quote.quote: I wouldn't use a helicopter like that to go so far over the sea. It sounds as if they were pushing it to the maximum
expert-quote.what: 'I wouldn't use a helicopter like that' is damning professional judgment - they made a basic error that any expert would avoid.
expert-quote.effect: Expert directly criticises their basic judgment.

excellent-irony.what: Claims of 'excellent' conditions after a crash create irony - either they're lying or can't handle even perfect conditions.
excellent-irony.effect: If conditions were excellent, the crash is even more damning.

taxpayer-bill.quote: The Ministry of Defence said the taxpayer would pick up the bill
taxpayer-bill.what: Official confirmation that 'the taxpayer would pick up the bill' validates the article's main criticism about wasted public money.
taxpayer-bill.effect: Confirms taxpayers will pay for their recklessness.

highly-unlikely.what: 'Highly unlikely' is bureaucratic speak for 'definitely not' - the money is gone forever.

wife-comment.quote: they'll probably have their bottoms kicked and be sent home the long way
wife-comment.what: The wife's comment about 'bottoms kicked' reduces the explorers to naughty schoolboys, ending on domestic comedy rather than heroic adventure.
wife-comment.effect: Final infantilisation - naughty boys getting punished.

farce.meaning: A complete failure or ridiculous situation
farce.note: Something absurd or ridiculous; a complete failure
farce.effect: Sets mocking tone from the very beginning.

intercept.note: To stop and catch something or someone before they reach their destination
intercept.effect: Suggests they were doing something wrong that needed stopping.

plunged.note: Fell or dived suddenly and uncontrollably

hostile.note: Unfriendly, antagonistic; (of environment) harsh and difficult to survive in

ditched.note: Made an emergency landing on water (aviation term)
ditched.effect: Technical term adds authenticity to report.

scrambled.note: Moved or climbed quickly and with difficulty, often in panic

dispatched.note: Sent off to a destination for a purpose

amphibious.note: Able to operate both on land and in water
amphibious.effect: Technical term showing sophisticated equipment they still failed with.

falmouth.meaning: a coastal town in Cornwall, England

overview.heading: Why Morris Wrote This Article
overview.intro: Morris's purposes are layered throughout the article:

points.label: To inform about the rescue
points.text: "The men were plucked from the icy water by a Chilean naval ship" - Basic news reporting

points.label: To criticise wasteful spending
points.text: "Last night there was resentment in some quarters" - Highlighting public anger

points.label: To question the explorers' judgment
points.text: "boys messing about with a helicopter" - Undermining their credibility

overview.heading: Who He's Writing For
overview.intro: Morris targets specific readers of The Guardian:

points.label: British taxpayers
points.text: "the taxpayers of Britain and Chile tens of thousands of pounds" - Direct relevance to those funding

points.label: Guardian readers (educated, liberal)
points.text: References to Jane's Helicopter Markets - assumes sophisticated knowledge

points.label: Critics of privilege
points.text: "property developer from London" - Class markers that resonate

overview.heading: Morris's Tone and Attitude
overview.intro: Notice how Morris's voice shifts between objective and critical:

points.label: Ironic headline
points.text: "Explorers or boys messing about?" - Immediately skeptical

points.label: Understated criticism
points.text: "not the first time they have hit the headlines for the wrong reasons" - Gentle mockery

overview.heading: Technical Choices
overview.intro: Morris uses specific language techniques to shape reader response:

points.label: Expert testimony
points.text: "I wouldn't use a helicopter like that" - Authority figures question decisions

points.label: Ironic juxtaposition
points.text: "nothing short of a miracle" vs "boys messing about" - Contrasting perspectives

overview.heading: How It's Organised
overview.intro: The article's structure builds the case against the explorers:

points.label: Hook with failure
points.text: "Their last expedition ended in farce" - Opens with previous incompetence

points.label: Cost emphasis
points.text: Rescue details followed immediately by "tens of thousands of pounds"

points.label: Pattern of failure
points.text: Current rescue → Past achievements → Previous failures - Undermining structure

points.label: Wife's punchline
points.text: "they'll probably have their bottoms kicked" - Ends with domestic comedy
